source_metadata.exact_title: A Multicenter, Randomized, Controlled Clinical Trial of Transfusion Requirements in Critical Care
authors: Transfusion Requirements in Critical Care Investigators for the Canadian Critical Care Trials Group
source_metadata.journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
corrections_applied: Page 412 enrollment comparison corrected to 20% cardiac disease among enrolled patients versus 26% among those not enrolled (P<0.01).
Page 413 wording corrected from P=0.15 and P=0.58 to P>0.15 and P>0.58 for similarity of cointerventions.

atoms.canonical_statement: The trial compared restrictive and liberal red-cell transfusion strategies to determine whether they produced equivalent 30-day mortality and organ-dysfunction outcomes in critically ill patients.
Eligible patients were expected to remain in the ICU for more than 24 hours, had hemoglobin <=9.0 g/dL within 72 hours after ICU admission, and were considered euvolemic after initial treatment.

population.label: Eligible critically ill ICU patients
inclusion_criteria: Hemoglobin <=9.0 g/dL within 72 hours after ICU admission

atoms.canonical_statement: Major exclusions included age <16 years, inability to receive blood products, active blood loss, chronic anemia, pregnancy, brain death or imminent death, consideration of withholding/withdrawing treatment, and routine cardiac surgical admission.

population.label: Excluded candidate ICU patients
exclusion_criteria: Question of withholding or withdrawing treatment

atoms.canonical_statement: Treatment assignment was stratified by center and APACHE II severity (<=15 vs >15) and balanced with permuted blocks of four or six using sequential sealed opaque envelopes prepared in computer-generated random order.
The restrictive strategy transfused red cells when hemoglobin fell below 7.0 g/dL and targeted 7.0-9.0 g/dL during the ICU stay.

exposures.details: Transfuse one red-cell unit at a time when hemoglobin falls below 7.0 g/dL; maintain hemoglobin 7.0-9.0 g/dL during the ICU stay.

atoms.canonical_statement: The liberal strategy transfused red cells when hemoglobin fell below 10.0 g/dL and targeted 10.0-12.0 g/dL during the ICU stay.

exposures.details: Transfuse when hemoglobin falls below 10.0 g/dL; maintain hemoglobin 10.0-12.0 g/dL during the ICU stay.

atoms.canonical_statement: The assigned transfusion strategy could not be masked from clinicians; other management decisions were left to treating physicians.
The primary outcome was death from all causes within 30 days after randomization.

Secondary outcomes included 60-day mortality, ICU and hospital mortality, survival time, organ failure/dysfunction measures, composite death-plus-organ-dysfunction outcomes, and ICU/hospital length of stay.
The final analysis was intention-to-treat; no adjustment was made for multiple comparisons, and the APACHE II subgroup threshold was changed in the final analysis from 15 to 20.
The trial was terminated early at 838 randomized patients after enrollment fell below 20% of predicted levels, despite a recalculated target sample size of 1620 patients.
Of 6451 patients assessed, 3206 were found eligible, 2039 were screened for consent, 838 consented and were randomized (418 restrictive, 420 liberal), and nine later withdrew.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that a restrictive red-cell transfusion strategy was at least as effective as and possibly superior to the liberal strategy in critically ill patients, with a possible exception for acute myocardial infarction and unstable angina.

The authors recommended transfusing critically ill patients when hemoglobin falls below 7.0 g/dL and maintaining hemoglobin between 7.0 and 9.0 g/dL, while cautioning about active coronary ischemic syndromes.

Because the transfusion strategy was not blinded, clinician behavior could potentially have influenced outcomes, although measured cointerventions were reported as similar after correction of the published P-value wording.

Only 41% of patients screened for consent were enrolled, and the authors noted that physician refusals were more common among patients with severe cardiac disease, limiting generalizability to active coronary ischemia.

The positive age and APACHE II subgroup findings require caution because the analysis used multiple subgroup comparisons without multiplicity adjustment and changed the APACHE II cut point from 15 to 20 in the final analysis.
